_comment: Hand-located readers for Hamlet, beyond Melville (who comes from MMO's XML).
Located by eye 2026-10-16. Milton: the Free Library of Philadelphia's First Folio,
archive.org/details/shk00001, Hamlet = Folio pp. 152-156 then 257-282 (the Folio skips
a hundred numbers), image index n763 = p. 152, n768 = p. 257. Keats: his own 7-vol
Dramatic Works (London, 1814-18), Houghton *EC8 K2262 Zz814s, vol. 7, Hamlet = IIIF
own page labels flag the marked pages '[contains marginalia]'. Spurgeon 1928 pp. 27-28
names five of his Hamlet passages; each is cited where she does.
Anchors are the TEXT of the line, never a line number. `span` = how many spoken lines
the bracket or underline runs over, from the anchor. Descriptions are plain; only words
a reader actually wrote are quoted.

annotators.name: John Milton
annotators.blurb: John Milton owned a First Folio identified in 2019 as his own, on the evidence of its handwriting. In Hamlet he did more than mark: he corrected the Folio's text, again and again writing in the margin the word that modern editions print. His corrections and brackets are reproduced here, located directly from the Free Library of Philadelphia's own digitization.
annotators.source: Free Library of Philadelphia's digitization of its 1623 First Folio, archive.org/details/shk00001; identification by Claire M. L. Bourne & Jason Scott-Warren (2019). No image is reproduced.

marks.anchor: When yond same star that's westward from the pole
marks.note: Bracketed in the margin: Bernardo's star, the bell beating one. Keats underlined the same lines.

marks.anchor: The cock, that is the trumpet to the morn,
marks.note: The Folio printed “the trumpet to the day.” Milton struck out “day” and wrote “morn” beside it, the word this text and modern editions print.

marks.anchor: MARCELLUS  It faded on the crowing of the cock.
marks.note: Bracketed: the bird of dawning that sings all night at Christmas. Keats underlined it too.

marks.anchor: But, look, the morn, in russet mantle clad,
marks.note: Bracketed with the speech before it: the morn in russet mantle.

marks.anchor: Hyperion to a satyr; so loving to my mother
marks.note: A long bracket down the first soliloquy, ending at “Frailty, thy name is woman.”

marks.anchor: By their oppress'd and fear-surprised eyes,
marks.note: The Folio printed “Be their opprest.” Milton crossed the “e” and wrote “by” in the margin. Keats underlined this line.

marks.anchor: Within his truncheon's length; whilst they, distilled
marks.note: Where the Folio has “bestil'd”, Milton marked the “be” and wrote “di” above it: distill'd, as this text reads.

marks.anchor: Do not, as some ungracious pastors do,
marks.note: Bracketed: Ophelia's answer, the primrose path of dalliance. Keats underlined the same lines.

marks.anchor: Be thy intents wicked or charitable,
marks.note: The Folio printed “Be thy euents”. Milton wrote “intents” in the margin.

marks.anchor: Or to the dreadful summit of the cliff
marks.note: Beside the Folio's “dreadfull Sonnet of the Cliffe” Milton wrote “sommet”: summit.

marks.anchor: And draw you into madness? think of it:
marks.note: Milton underlined “of it” and wrote “vide supple”, see the supplement. The Folio stops here; the four lines that follow in this text (“The very place puts toys of desperation…”) are not in it.

marks.anchor: With witchcraft of his wit, with traitorous gifts,--
marks.note: The Folio printed “hath Traitorous guifts.” Milton marked “hath” and wrote “with”.

marks.anchor: With juice of cursed hebenon in a vial,
marks.note: Milton wrote “hebona” beside the Folio's “Hebenon”, the poison's other spelling. This text keeps the Folio's.

marks.anchor: Tis now the very witching time of night,
marks.note: Bracketed: the very witching time of night.

marks.anchor: I, his sole son, do this same villain send
marks.note: The Folio printed “I his foule Sonne”. Milton marked it and wrote “sole”.

marks.anchor: HAMLET  Go, go, you question with a wicked tongue.
marks.note: The Folio has Hamlet echo his mother's “idle tongue”. Milton wrote “wicked” and boxed it.

marks.anchor: That you do bend your eye on vacancy
marks.note: The Folio printed “That you bend”. Milton put in “doe”, above the line and again in the margin.

marks.anchor: And with the incorporal air do hold discourse?
marks.note: The Folio printed “with their corporall ayre”. Milton struck “their” and began “in corpo…” in the margin, where the facsimile's page edge cuts it off.

marks.anchor: Yea, curb and woo for leave to do him good.
marks.note: Beside the Folio's “courb” Milton wrote “couch”. This text prints “curb”.

marks.anchor: Let the bloat king tempt you again to bed;
marks.note: The Folio printed “the blunt King”. Milton wrote “bloat”.

marks.anchor: And like the kind life-rendering pelican,
marks.note: The Folio printed “Life-rend'ring Politician”. Milton struck it through and wrote “Pelican”.

marks.anchor: QUEEN GERTRUDE  There is a willow grows aslant a brook,
marks.note: Bracketed, the whole of Gertrude's account of Ophelia's drowning. Keats underlined nearly every line of it.

marks.anchor: If thou didst ever hold me in thy heart
marks.note: Bracketed: absent thee from felicity awhile.

marks.anchor: HORATIO  Now cracks a noble heart. Good night sweet prince:
marks.note: Bracketed: Horatio's good night.

annotators.name: John Keats
annotators.blurb: John Keats read Hamlet in his own pocket Shakespeare, seven small volumes he owned from 1817, and ran his pen under the lines he loved. Caroline Spurgeon found the play “a good deal underlined” in 1928. The copy is now at Harvard's Houghton Library; the underlinings here were read from its digitization.
annotators.source: Keats's copy of The Dramatic Works of William Shakspeare (London, 1814-18), vol. 7, Houghton Library, Harvard, *EC8 K2262 Zz814s, digitized at nrs.harvard.edu/URN-3:FHCL.HOUGH:3425902; Caroline F. E. Spurgeon, Keats's Shakespeare (1928), pp. 27-28. No image is reproduced.

marks.anchor: When yond same star that's westward from the pole
marks.note: Underlined, to “The bell then beating one.”

marks.anchor: We do it wrong, being so majestical,
marks.note: Underlined.

marks.anchor: The bird of dawning singeth all night long:
marks.note: Underlined, “the exquisite line”, in Spurgeon's words.

marks.anchor: But, look, the morn, in russet mantle clad,
marks.note: Underlined: Horatio's sunrise, which Spurgeon singles out.

marks.anchor: HAMLET  O, that this too too solid flesh would melt
marks.note: Underlined, with a stroke down the margin beside the lines after it.

marks.anchor: Hyperion to a satyr; so loving to my mother
marks.note: Underlined, line after line, through the soliloquy.

marks.anchor: HAMLET  Thrift, thrift, Horatio! the funeral baked meats
marks.note: Underlined: the funeral baked meats.

marks.anchor: He was a man, take him for all in all,
marks.note: Underlined.

marks.anchor: By their oppress'd and fear-surprised eyes,
marks.note: Underlined, the line Milton corrected in his Folio.

marks.anchor: A violet in the youth of primy nature,
marks.note: Underlined, in the Laertes and Ophelia scene Spurgeon notes as marked.

marks.anchor: Too oft before their buttons be disclosed,
marks.note: Underlined: the morn and liquid dew of youth.

marks.anchor: Do not, as some ungracious pastors do,
marks.note: Underlined, every line. Milton bracketed the same speech.

marks.anchor: When I had seen this hot love on the wing--
marks.note: Underlined.

marks.anchor: Would, like the spring that turneth wood to stone,
marks.note: Marked, as Spurgeon prints it.

marks.anchor: And to such wondrous doing brought his horse,
marks.note: Underlined: the horseman incorpsed and demi-natured with the brave beast.

marks.anchor: There lives within the very flame of love
marks.note: Underlined: the wick or snuff that will abate it.

marks.anchor: QUEEN GERTRUDE  There is a willow grows aslant a brook,
marks.note: Underlined nearly line by line, to “To muddy death.” Milton bracketed it.

marks.anchor: Singeing his pate against the burning zone,
marks.note: Underlined: make Ossa like a wart.

marks.anchor: There's a divinity that shapes our ends,
marks.note: Underlined, with the lines before it.
